summary.short: Proposed New York bill amending the General Business Law. Requires controllers using solely automated decisions that materially contribute to denials of key services (finance, housing, insurance, health care, education, employment, necessities) to disclose this, offer appeals with 45-day responses, and conduct annual impact assessments by independent auditors.
summary.long: Proposed bill amending New York's General Business Law on the management and oversight of personal data. Under subdivision (A), a controller making an automated decision involving solely automated processing that materially contributes to denial of financial or lending services, housing, public accommodation, insurance, health care services, or access to basic necessities must disclose that the decision was made by a solely automated process, offer an appeal allowing the consumer to contest the decision, provide supporting information and obtain meaningful human review, and explain the appeal process. Controllers must respond to appeals within forty-five days, extendable once by forty-five days with notice and reasons. Under subdivision (C), controllers or processors engaged in automated decision-making in those fields, including those assisting others, must conduct an annual impact assessment describing objectives, design, training data, accuracy, fairness and bias testing, and assessing discriminatory results across protected characteristics. Assessments must use an external independent auditor or researcher, be publicly available online, be retained for at least six years, and be available to state, federal or local authorities on request. The excerpt states no effective date, penalties or enforcement authority, and it disapplies the jurisdictional limits of another section for these paragraphs.

notes: Excerpt only: the document contains the automated decision-making provision (paras (A) to (C)). It gives no section number, title or enacting article, and the text of section 1101 is not included. Bill title, status and stage come from registry metadata, not the document, and the document does not say it amends the General Business Law. Scope inconsistency: para (A) lists financial or lending services, housing, public accommodation, insurance, health care services and access to basic necessities, while (C)(I) also lists education enrollment and employment. Para (A) places duties on the controller, while (C) places them on the controller or processor. Para (A)(B) appeal-response periods are as stated in the text; no other relations are stated in this excerpt.
